weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.character: IdentityAccessManagement: the per-gateway, RWMutex-guarded identity store (singleton per S3ApiServer) plus the Auth middleware wrapping every S3 route; Identity/Account/Credential value types
gotchas: scrubInternalHeaders must run before any auth path; handlers trust headers like the object-lock, version-id and SSE key-material ones, and SeaweedFSPrincipalHeader is read back by buildPrincipalARN.
isEnabled() reads isAuthEnabled without the mutex, while writers set it under iam.m; once true it is never turned off.
DeleteObjects (POST ?delete with no object) skips per-request authorization here on purpose; DeleteMultipleObjectsHandler must call AuthorizeObjectDelete per key.
ListBuckets with an empty bucket defers authorization to the handler (per-bucket filtering), except for an anonymous identity with no List action, which is denied up front.
Groups in a static config file are ignored with a warning (groups are managed via the IAM API).
${VAR} references in a static file's keys are expanded from the environment; a credential with an unset or empty variable is dropped, not loaded literally.
LookupByAccessKey returns pointers into live maps: callers must not mutate them.
A native bare Admin action survives attaching IAM policies (#11226); only an explicit Deny in an attached policy removes it.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.if_broken: Requests are wrongly denied or allowed gateway-wide; revoked keys keep working; static admin credentials can disappear on a reload; the advanced-IAM engine evaluates stale policies.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.ux: Decides between 403 AccessDenied / InvalidAccessKeyId / SignatureDoesNotMatch and success for every client; determines whether an unconfigured `docker run seaweedfs` accepts anonymous requests.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.what: Holds every identity, access key, account, policy and group the gateway knows, loaded from up to three sources: a static -config/-iam.config file (immutable 'static' identities), the credential manager store (filer/Postgres, 'dynamic'), and AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET env vars (a static admin). Replace/Merge rebuild the in-memory maps atomically; UpsertIdentity, RemoveIdentity, PutPolicy and PutGroup apply pushed single changes. Auth(handler, action) is the middleware on each route: it scrubs internal headers, authenticates by auth type (SigV2, SigV4 header/presigned/streaming, JWT via IAM integration, anonymous) and authorizes. Authorization order: Phase-1 bucket policy (explicit Deny wins; Allow bypasses IAM unless an identity, group or session policy explicitly denies), then VerifyActionPermission via one of four routes (IAM integration, attached IAM policies, legacy 'Action:bucket/prefix' strings via CanDo, or deny). It also authorizes keys the URL does not name (copy source, DeleteObjects body keys, POST Object form key) on a synthesized request.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.when: Auth runs on every routed S3 request before the circuit breaker and handler. Config loads run at startup (file, then store with 10 retries at 2s, then env), on SIGHUP for the file, on filer metadata events via scheduleReload, every 1 min by polling for the Postgres store, and on gRPC pushes from peers (UpsertIdentity/RemoveIdentity/PutPolicy/PutGroup).
weed/s3api/auth_credentials.go.why: Consequence: this is the S3 security perimeter; every route is wrapped in iam.Auth, so a bug here is either an outage (everyone denied) or a breach (anyone allowed). Design: static identities cannot be overwritten by dynamic store reloads, but a config-file reload is authoritative for the identities that file declares, so a key revoked by editing the file stops authenticating without a restart. Loads are serialized end to end by reloadMu so an older snapshot cannot overwrite a newer one, and failed reloads retry every 5s, coalesced through a 1-slot channel. Pointing at a config file that yields no identities enables auth and denies everyone instead of falling open. With no config at all, auth stays off ('no credentials = allow all', #9557). AWS compatibility: bucket-policy Allow can grant what identity policies omit, but never overrides an explicit identity-side Deny; listings scope by ?prefix= only for list actions so an object-scoped grant cannot authorize bucket subresources; a denied authenticated request on a malformed bucket name answers InvalidBucketName like AWS.

weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.if_broken: Identities relying on policies from an advanced IAM file get AccessDenied, because their policies parse as empty.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.ux: Operators can use one IAM config file in either policy form; policies attached by name keep working.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.what: normalizeAdvancedIAMPolicies rewrites policies written in the advanced-IAM form {"name", "document": {...}} into the S3-config form {"name", "content": "<json string>"} before the protobuf parser sees the file. A document that is already a JSON string is used verbatim; an object is re-encoded as a string; anything it cannot rewrite is left untouched.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.when: Every static config load (loadS3ApiConfigurationFromBytes in auth_credentials.go), at startup and on SIGHUP.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_policy_docum.why: Consequence: with -s3.iam.config and no -s3.config, the same file is parsed as the S3 identity config; protojson silently drops the unknown 'document' field, leaving a policy with empty content that 'fails every later parse and takes the whole runtime policy sync down with it' (author comment). Design: the rewrite is all-or-nothing per policy, so a failure never strips a policy's only definition.

weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.character: S3ApiServer background loop: one long-lived filer metadata subscription per gateway that fans events out to cache and config refreshers
gotchas: The subscription is fatal-on-error per attempt and retried forever (util.RetryUntil with an always-true predicate); a broken filer means silent staleness, not a crash.
Handler errors are ignored (_ =); a failed refresh is only logged by the handler itself.
The circuit-breaker reload is triggered only for the exact file name in /etc/s3.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.if_broken: Gateways serve stale bucket configs (versioning, policies, CORS) and stale credentials (revoked keys keep working) until restart or TTL.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.ux: Bucket settings, IAM users/policies, OIDC providers and rate limits changed anywhere take effect on every gateway within moments.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.what: subscribeMetaEvents follows filer metadata events under /etc (plus BucketsPath and the IAM directories passed in by the constructor) from server start, retrying forever. For each event (handling renames as delete-from-old-dir plus create-in-new-dir) it calls: onBucketMetadataChange (bucket created/updated/deleted under BucketsPath → owner index maintenance, bucket-policy mirror into advanced IAM, BucketRegistry refresh/eviction, bucket config cache refresh of resident entries or invalidation), onIamConfigChange (identity file or identities/policies/service_accounts/groups dirs → coalesced IAM reload), onOIDCProviderChange (refresh OIDC providers from the store), onRoleChange (invalidate the role cache, honoring a custom role-store directory) and onCircuitBreakerConfigChange (/etc/s3/circuit_breaker.json → reload limits, reset on delete).
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.when: Started as a goroutine at the end of NewS3ApiServerWithStore and runs for the life of the process; each filer metadata event is processed synchronously, in order.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_subscribe.go.why: Consequence: this is what keeps every gateway's caches and IAM state consistent with changes made through any other gateway, the admin UI or weed shell; without it, bucket config would only refresh at the 60-minute cache TTL and IAM changes would need a restart. Design: config-cache updates only refresh buckets already resident (never warm the cache from events) and drop negative entries so a newly created bucket is visible at once; IAM changes schedule a coalesced full reload instead of applying partial diffs, so a burst of edits costs one reload.

weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.character: One IdentityAccessManagement method: a thin delegate to the advanced IAM integration
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.if_broken: Role assumption either always fails or ignores trust policies (privilege escalation).
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.ux: AccessDenied from AssumeRole when the role's trust policy does not name the caller.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.what: ValidateTrustPolicyForPrincipal(roleArn, principalArn) asks the IAM integration whether the role's trust policy lets that principal assume it, and fails with 'IAM integration not available' when there is none.
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.when: STS AssumeRole handling (s3api_sts.go) and the IAM middleware (s3_iam_middleware.go).
weed/s3api/auth_credentials_trust.go.why: Consequence: AssumeRole must check the target role's trust policy; without it any authenticated user could assume any role. Design: the trust evaluation lives in the advanced IAM manager (weed/iam), so the legacy identity store only forwards; failing closed when no integration exists means STS cannot grant roles without the engine that defines them.

weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.character: IdentityAccessManagement methods plus stateless helpers implementing legacy AWS Signature Version 2 (header, presigned query, POST policy); derived from MinIO
gotchas: Presigned V2 URLs have no maximum lifetime (SigV4 caps at 7 days).
When x-amz-date is present, the Date line in the string-to-sign is blanked (it is covered through the x-amz-* headers instead).
The invalid-access-key warnings log the full attempted access key id.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.if_broken: Legacy clients are locked out, or forged V2 requests are accepted.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.issue_note: Header-signed SigV2 requests are never checked for freshness: doesSignV2Match verifies the HMAC over the Date header but never compares that date to the server clock (the only RequestTimeTooSkewed check in the package is in the SigV4 header path). A captured V2-signed request can therefore be replayed indefinitely until the key is rotated, where AWS rejects V2 requests more than 15 minutes old. The canonical resource also omits subresources missing from resourceList (cors, tagging, object-lock, retention, legal-hold, encryption…), so a V2 signature for GET /bucket equally authenticates GET /bucket?cors or ?tagging.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.ux: Legacy V2 clients authenticate; failures answer SignatureDoesNotMatch / InvalidAccessKeyId / AccessDenied (expired presign).
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.what: Verifies 'Authorization: AWS <key>:<sig>' requests, presigned ?AWSAccessKeyId&Expires&Signature URLs and V2 POST-policy forms: looks up the key, rejects expired credentials, rebuilds the V2 string-to-sign (method, Content-MD5, Content-Type, Date or Expires, sorted x-amz-* headers, path plus the subresources in resourceList), computes HMAC-SHA1 and compares in constant time after base64-decoding both sides; records the access key id for audit.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.when: authenticateRequestInternal for authTypeSignedV2 / authTypePresignedV2; doesPolicySignatureV2Match from the POST Object handler.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v2.go.why: Consequence: older SDKs and tools (s3cmd defaults, legacy apps) still sign with V2; without this they cannot talk to the gateway. Design: constant-time comparison avoids a signature timing oracle; presigned expiry is checked before the key lookup. AWS compatibility: the canonical resource includes only the subresources AWS's V2 spec lists.

weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.character: IdentityAccessManagement methods plus stateless helpers implementing AWS Signature Version 4 verification (header, presigned query and POST-policy forms); derived from MinIO's implementation
gotchas: A Credential scope date that does not parse returns ErrMalformedCredentialDate, which has no s3err mapping and panics the error writer (see the s3err/ issue note).
Presigned requests check only expiry, not a future X-Amz-Date: ErrRequestNotReadyYet is never used, so a key holder can date a URL in the future and keep it valid well past 7 days from now.
X-Forwarded-Host/Port/Proto are tried as host candidates from any client (not only trusted proxies); this only changes which host the signature must cover, so it is not a bypass.
doesSignatureMatch and doesPresignedSignatureMatch are identical wrappers over verifyV4Signature(r, false).
The invalid-access-key warning logs the full attempted access key id.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.if_broken: All SigV4 clients fail, or forged / replayed requests are accepted.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.ux: SignatureDoesNotMatch, RequestTimeTooSkewed, AccessDenied (expired presign), InvalidAccessKeyId, ExpiredToken for clients; presigned URLs work behind reverse proxies when -s3.externalUrl or forwarded headers are set.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.what: verifyV4Signature: extract auth info (Credential scope, SignedHeaders, Signature, date) from the Authorization header or the X-Amz-* query → look up the access key (static identity) or, if absent and a session token is present, validate the STS session through the IAM integration → check presigned expiry → require every x-amz-* request header to be signed (verifySignedHeadersCoverage) → build the canonical request and recompute the HMAC chain, trying several host candidates (configured external host, X-Forwarded-Host/Port/Proto variants, Host) and path forms (original pre-rewrite path, escaped, decoded, and X-Forwarded-Prefix variants from trusted proxies only) → constant-time compare. Then it records the access key id in the context, and denies when a virtual-host-signed bucket differs from the routed bucket. Also validateSTSSessionToken (key id, expiry, non-empty principal; Iceberg-vended sessions must still be backed by a live, unchanged stored key) and doesPolicySignatureV4Match for POST Object.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.when: authenticateRequestInternal (auth_credentials.go) for SigV4 header, presigned and signed-streaming requests (the streaming chunk signatures are then checked in chunked_reader_v4.go); doesPolicySignatureV4Match from the POST Object handler.
weed/s3api/auth_signature_v4.go.why: Consequence: SigV4 is how nearly every SDK authenticates; an error here either locks out all clients or accepts forged requests. Design: real deployments sit behind proxies and ingresses that rewrite Host, port or path, so several host and path forms are tried; only X-Forwarded-Prefix is gated on trusted proxies, because it changes which path the signature covers. The virtual-host bucket check stops a request signed for bucket A on a.example.com from being routed to bucket B. Unsigned x-amz-* headers are rejected because handlers act on them (SSE, ACL, lock headers), except the presign protocol parameters and SSE-C key headers, which AWS SDKs leave unsigned on presigned URLs. A session token on a request signed by a static key is tolerated but ignored (some credential vendors, such as Unity Catalog, emit one with static keys). AWS compatibility: 15-minute clock-skew limit for header auth, 7-day (604800s) maximum presign expiry, non-s3 services (IAM/STS POSTs) have their body hashed up to a 10 MiB limit when no payload hash is sent.

weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.character: BucketRegistry: a second per-gateway bucket cache (LRU of BucketMetaData plus an LRU 'not found' set, with singleflight loading) focused on ownership and ACL; one instance per S3ApiServer
gotchas: The not-found set has no TTL: a bucket stays NoSuchBucket here until a metadata event (LoadBucketMetadata / RemoveBucketMetadata) or LRU eviction clears it; unlike BucketConfigCache's negative entries (ttl/4, at least 30s).
LoadBucketMetadata only refreshes buckets already in the cache; it never adds new ones.

Bucket ownership, owner and ACL are parsed from the same Extended keys here AND in newBucketConfigFromEntry (s3api_bucket_config.go), into two different caches with slightly different shapes (effective vs raw ownership); a change to one parse does not reach the other.
buildBucketMetadata JSON-marshals the whole (cipher-key-scrubbed) entry on every build, only for a debug log line.
loadBucketMetadataFromFiler is a package var so tests can stub the filer read.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.if_broken: Objects get the uploader instead of the bucket owner as owner (or vice versa), ACL-based access breaks, and table-bucket layout rules stop applying.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.ux: Invisible; it decides the Owner shown in listings and ACLs, and whether BucketOwnerEnforced takes effect.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.what: Caches, per bucket: whether it is an S3 Tables bucket, its effective ObjectOwnership (absent/invalid → BucketOwnerEnforced), its owner (account id from the owner key, else resolved from the creating identity name, else admin) and parsed ACL grants. GetBucketMetadata serves from cache, answers NoSuchBucket from the not-found set, or loads from the filer once per bucket even under concurrent misses (singleflight). LoadBucketMetadata/RemoveBucketMetadata are called by the metadata subscription to refresh or evict entries. bucketOwnerAccountId is shared with s3api_bucket_config.go.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.when: On object writes (owner stamping), ACL handlers, table-bucket checks (bucket_paths.go), and on every bucket create/update/delete event from the filer metadata subscription.
weed/s3api/bucket_metadata.go.why: Consequence: PutObject's object-owner decision (setObjectOwnerFromRequest), ACL checks and isTableBucket all ask this registry; a wrong answer makes objects owned by the wrong account or lets plain-object rules apply to a table bucket. Design: singleflight stops a thundering herd of filer lookups for a cold bucket; the cache is capped at bucketCacheCapacity (65536) so huge deployments keep only the hot set; owners recorded outside the S3 API (admin UI, weed shell) name an identity, which is resolved to its account here.

weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.character: S3ApiServer methods plus stateless package-level validators; one compiled regexp and two swappable package vars (clock, lookup) used as test seams
gotchas: bucketRoot ignores its bucket argument: all bucket types share option.BucketsPath.

isTableBucket fails open: any registry/filer error other than not-found is logged at V(1) and answered 'not a table bucket', so during a transient error a table bucket gets plain-bucket rules for the layout check.
Only PUT, GET, HEAD, DELETE and DeleteObjects accept the verify key; multipart, copy, rename, ACL, tagging and POST policy still apply the plain layout rule (author comment).
volumeVerifyNow and volumeVerifyLookup are package vars so tests can swap the clock and the lookup; read them at call time, never cache them.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.if_broken: A wrong bucketDir puts every object in, or reads it from, the wrong filer directory. isTableBucket returning true for a plain bucket rejects nearly every key; returning false for a table bucket lets arbitrary objects into it. A loosened verify-key check turns the exception into a way to store arbitrary data in table buckets.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.ux: Invisible for plain buckets. On a table bucket a client writing outside the Iceberg layout gets an InvalidIcebergLayout error, while Snowflake's volume verification succeeds.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.what: Says where a bucket lives in the filer (bucketDir = BucketsPath/<bucket>, bucketPrefix, getBucketEntry, bucketExists) and enforces the S3 Tables object layout: in a table bucket an object must sit under namespace/table/{data|metadata}/… or be a table marker file at namespace/table/<marker>. It also carves out one narrow exception, the Snowflake external-volume verification key verify_<13-digit epoch ms>_<n> at the bucket root.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.when: getBucketEntry/bucketExists run for bucket-scoped requests and config loads; validateTableBucketObjectPath(OrVerify) runs inside object read/write handlers for every key of a table bucket; volumeVerifyPutAllowed gates the PUT handler only when the key matched the verify shape.
weed/s3api/bucket_paths.go.why: Consequence: every handler builds filer paths through bucketDir/bucketPrefix, so this decides where every object is read and written; getBucketEntry refuses dot-prefixed names so internal trees under /buckets (.system) can never be addressed as a bucket. Design: isTableBucket asks the in-memory bucketRegistry first and only falls back to a filer lookup when there is no registry. AWS/ecosystem compatibility: Snowflake's SYSTEM$VERIFY_EXTERNAL_VOLUME writes, reads, lists and deletes a 21-byte verify_… object at the volume root before using it; without the exception a table bucket cannot be a Snowflake external volume. The exception is fenced so it cannot store data: bucket root only, one regex shape, never a directory, PUT dated within ±1h of the server clock, Content-Length ≤ 1024 with no chunked/undeclared body, no user metadata, tagging, stored content headers or zip extraction.

weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.character: The leader-elected background loop that publishes bucket size metrics and enforces bucket quotas by flipping buckets read-only
gotchas: Enforcement lags by up to a minute plus vacuum, so a bucket can overshoot its quota by a minute of writes.
Every gateway uses the same lock owner string (<filer>-s3-metrics), so log lines about the owner cannot tell gateways apart; the renew token still keeps only one holder.
Without -master the loop silently does nothing, so quotas are never enforced.
The lock goes through Filers[0] only; if that filer is down no gateway collects metrics or enforces quotas.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.if_broken: Quotas stop being enforced (or never lift), and size dashboards go stale.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.ux: Prometheus shows per-bucket size; a bucket at quota starts refusing writes shortly after crossing it and accepts them again after deletes and vacuum.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.what: startBucketSizeMetricsLoop waits 10s, then holds a long-lived distributed lock 's3.leader' through the first filer. Every minute, while it holds the lock, it asks a master for CollectionStatistics, lists the buckets, sets each bucket's logical size, physical size and object-count gauges, and calls enforceBucketQuotas. That function reads filer.conf, flips each bucket's read-only flag to match LogicalSize() against its quota (ApplyBucketQuotaReadOnly) and saves filer.conf only when a flag changed.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.when: Started from the server constructor as a goroutine; runs every minute for the life of the process, only on the gateway holding the lock.
weed/s3api/bucket_size_metrics.go.why: Consequence: quotas are enforced here, not on the write path: a bucket over quota becomes read-only within about a minute, and a bucket under quota is writable again. Design: the master summarises collection statistics so the gateway does not pull every volume each minute. The leader lock keeps several gateways from rewriting filer.conf at once. LogicalSize subtracts un-vacuumed deleted bytes so vacuum lag never counts against a bucket, matching the Admin UI.

weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.character: s3ChunkedReader: a per-request io.ReadCloser state machine that decodes aws-chunked upload bodies (derived from MinIO), plus the ChecksumAlgorithm enum and hash constructors used across the write path
gotchas: If several x-amz-checksum-* lines appear in the trailer, the last one wins.
Close() is a no-op; the caller closes the underlying body.
ChecksumAlgorithm/getCheckSumWriter defined here are also used by putToFiler and multipart checksum computation.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.if_broken: Objects are stored with framing garbage, uploads fail for modern SDKs, or tampered bodies are accepted.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.issue_note: For STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD-TRAILER uploads the body is not authenticated. Chunk signatures are only checked when a chunk line carries ';chunk-signature=' (an absent signature is simply skipped), and in trailer mode the final chunk goes straight to the trailer checksum, so neither the last chunk signature nor x-amz-trailer-signature is ever verified. Reproduced against this commit with a throwaway test: a reader built as newChunkedReader builds it with auth on (credential set, hasTrailer) returned an attacker-chosen body without error when the chunks carried no signatures and the trailer carried a matching CRC32. The header (seed) signature still has to be valid, so this is a body-integrity gap (replay of captured headers within the 15-minute window, or MITM on plain HTTP), not an authentication bypass. Without a trailer, a missing final-chunk signature does fail.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.ux: Streaming uploads from modern SDKs work; corrupt or tampered chunks fail with chunk-signature / checksum mismatch errors.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.what: newChunkedReader verifies the request's SigV4 header signature (the seed signature) for signed streaming uploads and returns a reader that strips the aws-chunked framing ('<hex size>;chunk-signature=<sig>\r\n<data>\r\n'), recomputes each chunk's signature as an HMAC chained from the previous one, hashes the payload with the advertised trailer checksum (CRC32, CRC32C, CRC64NVME, SHA1, SHA256), and checks the trailer 'x-amz-checksum-*' line against it. It also handles STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER (no chunk signatures, checksum only). Chunk header lines are capped at 4 KiB.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.when: getRequestDataReader (s3api_put_object_helper.go) for PUT / UploadPart bodies whose x-amz-content-sha256 is a STREAMING-* value.
weed/s3api/chunked_reader_v4.go.why: Consequence: SDKs upload large or streaming bodies (aws-cli, boto3, Java SDK v2 with checksums) in aws-chunked framing; without this decoder the stored object would contain the framing bytes. Design: chained chunk signatures are what authenticate the BODY of a streaming SigV4 upload, since the header signature covers only the literal STREAMING-... payload marker; trailer checksums give end-to-end integrity for unsigned streaming. AWS compatibility: the signed, signed-trailer and unsigned-trailer streaming variants and the five flexible checksum algorithms.

weed/s3api/cors/.character: The CORS engine as a package of its own: the bucket CORSConfiguration types, their validation, rule matching, and the middleware that answers preflights and decorates responses
gotchas: The response always echoes the request Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, even for a '*' rule (AWS answers '*' without credentials).
A preflight whose method or headers are not allowed still gets 200 with Allow-Origin but no Allow-Methods; the browser blocks it, but it is not the 403 AWS sends.
Non-preflight requests are served even when no rule matches; only the CORS headers are withheld, and the browser hides the response.
weed/s3api/cors/.if_broken: Browser uploads and downloads fail with CORS errors, or responses become readable from origins the bucket owner never allowed.
weed/s3api/cors/.issue_note: EvaluateRequest stops at the first rule whose AllowedOrigins match, and for a preflight it builds the response from that rule even when its AllowedMethods (or AllowedHeaders) do not cover the request. AWS picks the first rule that matches origin AND method AND headers. A common configuration therefore fails: rule 1 {origins:[*], methods:[GET]}, rule 2 {origins:[https://app.example.com], methods:[PUT,POST]}. Probe (cors package test): a PUT preflight from https://app.example.com → allowOrigin set, allowMethods "" (browser blocks the upload); the actual PUT request evaluated without a preflight → allowMethods "PUT, POST". Only the actual-request path checks the method before accepting a rule.
weed/s3api/cors/.ux: Browsers get Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers/Expose-Headers/Max-Age as configured; a disallowed preflight fails in the browser console.
weed/s3api/cors/.what: cors.go defines CORSRule / CORSConfiguration (XML and JSON), ValidateConfiguration (1–100 rules; methods limited to GET/PUT/POST/DELETE/HEAD; at most one origin wildcard, only after http:// or https://), ParseRequest, EvaluateRequest (first rule whose origin matches; for actual requests the method must match too), the preflight and actual response builders, and ApplyHeaders. middleware.go wraps every request. It reads the bucket's CORS configuration through an interface, falls back to a global configuration when the bucket has none or does not exist, adds 'Vary: Origin', answers OPTIONS preflights itself (403 when nothing matches), and lets non-preflight requests through even when no rule matches.
weed/s3api/cors/.when: Every S3 request through the router-level middleware and every OPTIONS preflight; ValidateConfiguration on PutBucketCors.
weed/s3api/cors/.why: Consequence: browsers block every cross-origin upload or download that does not get the right Access-Control-* headers, so web apps that talk to S3 directly depend on this. Design: the engine sits behind small interfaces (BucketChecker, CORSConfigGetter) so it does not import the gateway, and a missing bucket falls back to the global configuration instead of a 403, so a preflight cannot reveal whether a bucket exists. AWS compatibility: rule shape, validation limits and wildcard rules follow PutBucketCors. Expose '*' is expanded to the standard S3 headers because browsers treat '*' literally on credentialed requests.

weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.character: Single stateless exported mapping function shared with weed/iamapi
gotchas: Any new permanent credential error (e.g. a duplicate policy) must be added here, or it surfaces as ServiceFailure (HTTP 500).
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.if_broken: IAM tooling misreads failures (retries forever on a missing user, or treats a duplicate as a server error).
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.ux: IAM clients get EntityAlreadyExists / NoSuchEntity instead of a generic failure, so idempotent tooling works.
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.what: CredentialErrToIamErrCode maps credential-store errors to IAM error codes: ErrUserAlreadyExists → EntityAlreadyExists, ErrUserNotFound / ErrAccessKeyNotFound → NoSuchEntity, anything else → ServiceFailure.
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.when: Embedded IAM API handlers (s3api_embedded_iam.go) and weed/iamapi management handlers, whenever a credential-manager call fails.
weed/s3api/credential_iam_errors.go.why: Consequence: IAM clients (aws iam ..., Terraform) branch on these codes; without the mapping every store error would look like a 500, or worse, a store failure could be reported as a 200. Design: one function shared by the standalone IAM server (weed/iamapi) and the embedded IAM API, so the two report identical error granularity. AWS compatibility: the codes are the AWS IAM exception names.

weed/s3api/custom_types.go.character: A single result struct for the conditional-header checks (If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Unmodified-Since)
gotchas: Entry is nil both when the object does not exist and when the check did not need to fetch it; callers must not read nil as 'absent'.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.if_broken: Conditional requests answer from a stale or missing entry: wrong 304/412 decisions, or delete-marker 404s without their headers.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.ux: Invisible: it decides whether a client gets 200, 304 or 412.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.what: Defines ConditionalHeaderResult: the S3 error code the check decided, the object's ETag (for a 304), the entry it fetched while checking (so the handler does not look it up again) and, when the resolved key is a delete marker, that marker's entry so a missing-key answer can still carry its headers.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.when: Returned by the conditional-header evaluators the object read and write handlers call before streaming or writing.
weed/s3api/custom_types.go.why: Consequence: GET, HEAD, PUT and CopyObject all evaluate conditions before acting. Returning the fetched entry saves a second filer lookup, and that lookup could see a different version than the one the condition was checked against. AWS compatibility: a 404 on a delete marker must still return x-amz-delete-marker and the version ID, which is why the marker is carried through.

weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.character: S3ApiServer methods implementing multipart upload storage on the filer: create, complete, abort, list uploads and parts, plus the ETag/checksum math
gotchas: Completion copies ALL Extended keys of the upload entry onto the object (except the key marker), so whatever createMultipartUpload stores (including object-lock fields; see the s3api_object_handlers_multipart.go issue) ends up on the object.
SSE-S3 per-chunk IVs are derived from each chunk's PART-local offset with no part term, mirroring putToFiler's partOffset=0 (see the s3api_put_handlers.go issue about keystream reuse).
Duplicate uploads of the same part number are resolved by the newest first-chunk ModifiedTsNs; the losers are deleted after commit.
listMultipartUploads lists the whole .uploads folder (math.MaxInt32 limit) on every call and keeps only a heap of the page.
The non-versioned path marks the object SeaweedFSExpiresS3 when any part carried a TTL.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.if_broken: Completed objects with missing or misordered bytes, wrong ETags that break SDK verification, orphaned part data, or chunks freed under a live object.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.issue_note: completeMultipartUpload builds the final entry three times with near-identical decorate closures (versioned decorateVersionEntry, suspended, non-versioned): upload id, parts count, part boundaries, owner, copying the upload entry's Extended, first-part SSE headers, SSE-S3 headers, ETag, checksum, mime, size. A fix to what a completed object carries must be made in all three.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.ux: Large-object uploads complete with AWS-compatible ETags and checksums; retries of Complete are safe; aborts free storage.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.what: createMultipartUpload makes <bucket>/.uploads/<uploadId> (id = sha1(key)_<uuid hex>) holding the key, owner, user metadata, ACL, checksum algorithm/type, object-lock metadata and the multipart encryption config (SSE-KMS key id/context/base IV, or SSE-S3 shared DEK + base IV, chosen from headers or the bucket default). completeMultipartUpload validates part order, ETags and sizes (non-last parts ≥5 MiB), stitches part chunks into one chunk list with rebased offsets (backfilling SSE-S3 per-chunk IVs when missing), records part boundaries and parts count, computes the multipart ETag md5(concat(part md5s))-N and COMPOSITE or FULL_OBJECT checksums (CRC combine), manifestizes chunks, and commits by versioning state: a new version under .versions/ (routed finalize transaction or mkFile + pointer update), a 'null' object for suspended buckets, or a plain object, each removing the upload dir in the same transaction when routed. A retried Complete after a commit is answered from the stored object (SeaweedFSUploadId). abortMultipartUpload deletes the upload dir under the object lock, keeping chunks if the upload was in fact completed. listMultipartUploads keeps a bounded heap of the next page; listObjectParts pages part files.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.when: CreateMultipartUpload, CompleteMultipartUpload, AbortMultipartUpload, ListParts, ListMultipartUploads (via s3api_object_handlers_multipart.go); routedUploadRemoval/writeMultipartObject from s3api_object_routed_write.go.
weed/s3api/filer_multipart.go.why: Consequence: this is where large objects become real objects; a bug corrupts or loses large uploads, or deletes chunks still referenced by a completed object. Design: abort checks whether the upload was already completed (an object or version carrying its upload id) and then removes only metadata, because the completed object shares the part chunks; the routed abort uses an IF_EXTENDED_NOT_EQUAL condition on the object for the same reason. Completion is idempotent so SDK retries after a lost response succeed instead of answering NoSuchUpload. Manifest chunks folded during completion are tracked so they are deleted on failure and kept on success. AWS compatibility: multipart ETag format '<md5>-<parts>', InvalidPartOrder, EntityTooSmall, InvalidPart, COMPOSITE vs FULL_OBJECT checksum types (CRC64NVME full-object only; SHA1/SHA256 composite only).

weed/s3api/filer_util.go.character: S3ApiServer methods: the gateway's basic filer CRUD vocabulary (mkdir/mkFile/list/rm/getEntry/updateEntry), with stateless retry helpers
gotchas: Most helpers use context.Background(); only rm/rmObject take a ctx (consumed by retryFilerOp and the DeleteEntry RPC).
listRetry may re-deliver entries a failed attempt already saw: a doList that accumulates must reset its slice first (listWithRetry does; routed_read's listing resets explicitly).
isReservedDirectoryName names are never turned into prefix objects by mkFile.
clearDirectoryMarkerMetadata keeps only xattr-* and SeaweedFS-internal extended keys and drops the prefix-object flag; anything else stored on the marker is lost when it is demoted.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.if_broken: Retrying non-transient list errors would add latency to every miss; not retrying deletes resurfaces flaky 500s; a broken prefix-object path makes PutObject on a key that already has children fail with 'existing is directory'.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.ux: Invisible. It is why a transient filer hiccup does not show up as InternalError on deletes and listings, and why keys like 'photos' and 'photos/1.jpg' can coexist.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.what: Wraps filer_pb calls into the small set of operations handlers use: mkdir, mkdirExclusive (never replaces an existing entry), mkFile (retries as a 'prefix object' on the directory when other keys are nested under the name), list with bounded retries, rm/rmObject with idempotent-delete retries, exists, getEntry, updateEntry, getCollectionName (FilerGroup_bucket) and objectKey. rmObject turns a non-empty explicit directory marker into a plain implicit directory instead of failing.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.when: Called by nearly every handler and background loop for raw filer access; list() backs bucket and object listings, rm/rmObject back DeleteObject(s) and DeleteBucket, mkdirExclusive backs PutBucket.
weed/s3api/filer_util.go.why: Design: listings retry up to 3 times (100ms then 200ms backoff) only on transient gRPC statuses, never on not-found, because a listing has no side effects and collects into a fresh slice per attempt. Deletes retry because the filer answers 'already gone' with an empty error, so a dropped reply can be re-sent safely; otherwise a lost reply would become a 500 on DeleteBucket or a per-key InternalError inside a DeleteObjects 200, which no SDK retries. mkdirExclusive exists so PutBucket cannot replace a table bucket created in its check-to-create window. AWS compatibility: S3 allows both 'a' and 'a/b' as keys; the filer cannot have a file and a directory with one name, so mkFile marks the directory itself as the object (MarkPrefixObject), and deleting such a directory key strips its object metadata (demoteDirectoryMarkerToImplicitDirectory) while keeping xattr-* and internal keys.

weed/s3api/lifecycle_xml/.character: The BucketLifecycleConfiguration XML wire form as a dependency-light package, plus the converter to and from the engine's flat s3lifecycle.Rule
gotchas: The canonical form has no transitions: LifecycleToCanonical drops Transition and NoncurrentVersionTransition, and MarshalCanonical cannot write them back.
Rule holds one Transition, not a list; a rule with several <Transition> elements keeps only the last.
flattenFilter gives a direct <Tag> priority over a sibling <Prefix> in the same Filter (AWS would reject that document), and Prefix.UnmarshalXML ignores its decode error.
weed/s3api/lifecycle_xml/.if_broken: Objects expire under the wrong prefix or tag filter, or never expire, and configurations do not round-trip.
weed/s3api/lifecycle_xml/.ux: Lifecycle documents written with aws-cli or Terraform are understood the same way everywhere; documents written by tooling come back with the namespace clients expect.
weed/s3api/lifecycle_xml/.what: types.go defines Lifecycle / Rule / Filter / And / Expiration / Transition / NoncurrentVersion* / AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload. Each has custom (Un)MarshalXML that records whether the element was present, so an absent element and an empty one differ, and Filter accepts Prefix | Tag | And plus size bounds. canonical.go has Parse / ParseCanonical, LifecycleToCanonical (Filter first, the legacy top-level Prefix as fallback), CanonicalToLifecycle / MarshalCanonical (choosing the narrowest Filter shape, sorted And tags, stamping the S3 namespace) and flattenFilter.
weed/s3api/lifecycle_xml/.when: PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration validation, the fast-path TTL resolver and warning, the lifecycle worker and scheduler, and shell commands that read or write lifecycle rules.
weed/s3api/lifecycle_xml/.why: Consequence: the gateway stores the client's lifecycle XML and the lifecycle worker, the TTL fast path and weed shell all interpret it, so two parsers that disagree would expire different objects than the user configured. Design: kept outside weed/s3api so the shell and the worker can parse the same shape without importing the gateway (weed/s3api pulls in weed/server, which imports weed/shell). The set flags let a round trip reproduce what the client sent. AWS compatibility: element names, the Filter/And rules and the legacy Prefix form follow the S3 API.

weed/s3api/object_lock_utils.go.character: Stateless helpers: the on-entry storage format of bucket versioning and object-lock configuration, and validation of retention / legal-hold / lock-configuration documents
gotchas: ExtractObjectLockInfoFromConfig converts Years to days as Years*365 (no leap days).
StoreObjectLockConfigurationInExtended(nil) deletes the lock keys, but updateBucketConfig never passes nil, so object lock cannot be turned off once enabled.
weed/s3api/object_lock_utils.go.if_broken: Buckets lose or misreport their object-lock defaults, new objects get no default retention, or invalid configurations are accepted.
weed/s3api/object_lock_utils.go.ux: Correct ObjectLockConfiguration round-trips and the AWS error codes for malformed lock documents (MalformedXML, InvalidRetentionPeriod, InvalidRequest).
weed/s3api/object_lock_utils.go.what: Stores the bucket's ObjectLockConfiguration as individual Extended keys (Seaweed-X-Amz-Object-Lock-Enabled, Lock-Default-Mode / -Days / -Years) instead of XML, and loads it back (also accepting the legacy value 'true' for Enabled). Converts to and from the (enabled, mode, duration-days) form other subsystems use, and validates: a retention needs Mode ∈ {GOVERNANCE, COMPLIANCE} and a future RetainUntilDate; a legal hold must be ON/OFF; a lock configuration must say Enabled, and a default retention needs a mode and exactly one of Days/Years, positive and within 36500 days / 100 years. HasObjectsWithActiveLocks / CheckBucketForLockedObjects delegate to the s3_objectlock package.
weed/s3api/object_lock_utils.go.when: PutBucket with x-amz-bucket-object-lock-enabled, Get/PutObjectLockConfiguration, PutObjectRetention / LegalHold validation, bucket config loads, DeleteBucket's locked-object check.
weed/s3api/object_lock_utils.go.why: Consequence: these keys are how the gateway decides whether a bucket is WORM; mis-storing them silently disables retention for new objects. Design: storing components rather than XML lets the config cache (newBucketConfigFromEntry) parse lock state without an XML decode on every request, and lets other components (admin UI, s3_objectlock) read the same keys. AWS compatibility: the validation mirrors S3's PutObjectLockConfiguration / PutObjectRetention rules; days and years are mutually exclusive and zero is invalid.

weed/s3api/policy/.character: Leaf package (derived from MinIO) for browser POST Object upload policies: parse the base64-decoded policy JSON and check form fields against it; stateless
gotchas: content-length-range is only parsed here (ContentLengthRange); enforcing it is up to the caller.
Field names are matched in canonical header form; condition keys are lower-cased with a '$' prefix.
weed/s3api/policy/.if_broken: Signed upload forms can be abused to write other keys, set public ACLs or oversized objects, or valid forms are rejected.
weed/s3api/policy/.ux: HTML-form uploads to S3 work and are constrained exactly as the issuing server signed them.
weed/s3api/policy/.what: ParsePostPolicyForm reads {expiration, conditions} where each condition is a {field: value} map (exact match), an [op, $field, value] triple with eq / starts-with, or [content-length-range, min, max]. CheckPostPolicy rejects an expired policy; rejects any X-Amz-* form field the policy does not mention (except the signing fields), with 'starts-with $x-amz-meta-' style prefix rules covering families of fields; verifies every condition against the form (starts-with is allowed only on fields AWS allows it for, e.g. $key, $content-type, $acl, not $bucket); and rejects unknown condition keys.
weed/s3api/policy/.when: PostPolicyBucketHandler (s3api_object_handlers_postpolicy.go) after the form signature is verified.
weed/s3api/policy/.why: Consequence: a POST policy is the only thing limiting what an anonymous browser holding a signed form may upload; a loose check lets the holder write any key, ACL or metadata. Design: unknown X-Amz-* fields are refused ('Extra input fields') so signed-for metadata cannot be widened. AWS compatibility: condition syntax, the starts-with field whitelist and error wording follow AWS's POST policy spec.

weed/s3api/policy_engine/.character: Neighbor package: an AWS-IAM-style policy engine (parse, compile, evaluate policy documents) used for bucket policies and for locally attached IAM policies; PolicyEngine instances hold compiled policies keyed by bucket or policy name behind an RWMutex
gotchas: An unsupported condition operator makes the condition false; for a Deny statement that means the Deny silently does not apply (bucket policies are validated on Put, but IAM policies loaded from stores are not).
Multipart sub-actions (UploadPart, Complete, Abort, ListParts) match statements that grant s3:PutObject.
UploadPart/UploadPartCopy inherit the SSE algorithm chosen at CreateMultipartUpload for s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption conditions.
Grant-header conditions (s3:x-amz-grant-*) are also checked against the original pre-normalization header values for Deny statements.
examples.go in this directory is excluded (//go:build ignore).
weed/s3api/policy_engine/.if_broken: Policies stop granting or denying correctly gateway-wide.
weed/s3api/policy_engine/.issue_note: s3:authType is only set for header-signed requests (REST-HEADER) and SigV2 presigned URLs (?AWSAccessKeyId → REST-QUERY-STRING). A SigV4 presigned URL (?X-Amz-Credential, what current SDKs generate) gets no s3:authType at all, so AWS's documented 'deny presigned URLs' policy (Deny with StringEquals s3:authType REST-QUERY-STRING) does not stop them. Reproduced with a throwaway test against this commit: the same Deny statement returned Deny for a SigV2 presigned request and Allow for a SigV4 presigned one. POST Object uploads likewise never get s3:authType=POST.
weed/s3api/policy_engine/.ux: AWS-style policies work as written, including IP and tag conditions.
weed/s3api/policy_engine/.what: types.go parses policy JSON (Version, Statement with Effect, Action/NotAction, Resource/NotResource, Principal/NotPrincipal, Condition) and compiles patterns into regexps / wildcard matchers, keeping ${...} variable patterns for per-request substitution. engine.go evaluates: a statement matches when action (multipart sub-actions also match s3:PutObject grants), resource / not-resource, principal / not-principal and all conditions match; any matching Deny wins, otherwise Allow if any Allow matched, else Indeterminate. It extracts request condition keys (aws:SourceIp via trusted proxies, aws:SecureTransport, times, user agent, referer, s3:prefix/delimiter/max-keys, s3:authType, s3:RequestMethod, every x-amz-* header as s3:x-amz-*, s3:RequestObjectTag/*) and principal variables from ARNs (aws:username, aws:userid, aws:PrincipalAccount, aws:principaltype); substitutes ${aws:*}, ${jwt:*}, ${ldap:*}. conditions.go implements String*, Numeric*, Date*, Bool, IpAddress, Arn*, Null and ForAllValues/ForAnyValue operators, s3:ExistingObjectTag/* from the object entry. trusted_proxies.go resolves the client IP from X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-Ip only for configured proxy peers; bucket_policy.go validates a bucket policy (Principal required, resources inside the bucket, s3: actions only, known operators, 20 KiB max).
weed/s3api/policy_engine/.when: BucketPolicyEngine (s3api_bucket_policy_engine.go) on bucket-policy evaluation; IdentityAccessManagement.iamPolicyEngine for attached/group policies; validation on PutBucketPolicy.
weed/s3api/policy_engine/.why: Consequence: every bucket policy and every attached IAM policy decision in the gateway comes from this engine; an error is either a data exposure or a lockout. Design: policies are compiled once on load and evaluated per request without re-parsing; deny-overrides-allow and Indeterminate let callers layer resource and identity policies AWS-style; forwarded headers are trusted only from configured proxies so aws:SourceIp cannot be spoofed by clients. AWS compatibility: policy grammar, operators, condition keys and variables follow AWS IAM so policies can be copied from AWS.

weed/s3api/request_body.go.character: A bounded body reader shared by the handlers that must read a whole request body into memory
gotchas: The body has been consumed afterwards; callers that pass the request on (UnifiedPostHandler) must put the bytes back in r.Body themselves.
s3tables has its own readRequestBody method with a fixed 10 MB cap; it is not this function.
weed/s3api/request_body.go.if_broken: Unbounded allocation on attacker-sized bodies, or valid bodies at exactly the limit rejected.
weed/s3api/request_body.go.ux: Oversized configuration bodies are refused instead of slowing or crashing the gateway.
weed/s3api/request_body.go.what: readRequestBody reads at most limit+1 bytes through an io.LimitReader and returns errRequestBodyTooLarge when the body is longer than limit; a nil body yields nil.
weed/s3api/request_body.go.when: UnifiedPostHandler (10 MiB IAM limit), SigV4 body hashing for IAM/STS requests, PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration, PutBucketQuota and PutBucketRequestPayment.
weed/s3api/request_body.go.why: Consequence: XML and form bodies (lifecycle configuration, quota, request payment, the IAM/STS POST body, the SigV4 payload hash for non-S3 services) are read fully before parsing, so without a cap one request could exhaust the gateway's memory. Design: reading one byte past the limit tells 'exactly at the limit' apart from 'too large' without trusting Content-Length.

weed/s3api/s3_action_resolver.go.character: Stateless resolver from (HTTP method, query subresources, bucket/object shape, legacy action) to the fine-grained AWS s3: action string
gotchas: The bucket-subresource table is a Go map iterated in random order: a request naming two subresources would resolve nondeterministically; rejectAmbiguousSubresource (router middleware) exists so such requests never get here.
Unknown legacy actions fall back to 's3:'+action rather than failing.
weed/s3api/s3_action_resolver.go.if_broken: Policies grant or deny the wrong operations, e.g. a GetObject grant that also allows reading ACLs, or version deletes allowed by a DeleteObject grant.
weed/s3api/s3_action_resolver.go.ux: AWS IAM / bucket policies written with fine-grained actions behave as on AWS.
weed/s3api/s3_action_resolver.go.what: ResolveS3Action maps a request to the action IAM and bucket policies are written against: multipart operations by uploadId/uploads/partNumber; ?acl, ?tagging, ?attributes with version-specific variants when versionId is present; GetObjectVersion / DeleteObjectVersion for versioned reads/deletes; ListBucketVersions, ListBucket (incl. list-type=2); a table of bucket subresources (policy, cors, lifecycle, versioning, notification, object-lock, encryption, requestPayment, publicAccessBlock, ownershipControls); location, retention, legal-hold, DeleteObjects, the SeaweedFS quota extension; then plain object/bucket method mapping; finally a legacy-action fallback (Read→GetObject, Write→PutObject, Admin→s3:*, …). Explicit object-lock actions and iam:/sts: actions pass through unchanged.
weed/s3api/s3_action_resolver.go.when: Inside every policy evaluation (BucketPolicyEngine.EvaluatePolicy, evaluateAttachedIAMPolicies, resolveS3AuthTarget, deferAnonymousObjectRead, putObjectACLPolicyRequest).
weed/s3api/s3_action_resolver.go.why: Consequence: the legacy route actions (Read/Write/List/Admin) are too coarse for AWS-style policies; without this, a policy allowing s3:GetObject could not tell a GET from a GET ?acl, or a DELETE from a DELETE ?versionId. Design: one resolver feeds bucket policies, attached IAM policies and the advanced IAM integration, so all three evaluate the same action. AWS compatibility: DELETE of lifecycle/encryption/publicAccessBlock/ownershipControls requires the corresponding Put permission, as in AWS.

weed/s3api/s3_bucket_encryption.go.character: S3ApiServer HTTP handlers for Get/Put/DeleteBucketEncryption plus the accessor the write path uses to find a bucket's default encryption
gotchas: PutBucketEncryptionHandler reads the body with an unbounded io.ReadAll (lifecycle uses a size-limited readRequestBody).
GetBucketEncryptionHandler encodes the XML directly with xml.NewEncoder (no XML declaration, no s3err success writer or PostLog).
IsDefaultEncryptionEnabled and GetDefaultEncryptionHeaders have no callers.
Stored in Entry.Content together with tags and CORS, so a concurrent tagging or CORS write is a last-write-wins race on the same blob (see s3api_bucket_config.go).
weed/s3api/s3_bucket_encryption.go.if_broken: Default encryption silently stops applying (compliance risk) or every write to such buckets fails.
weed/s3api/s3_bucket_encryption.go.ux: Bucket default encryption behaves like AWS's: new objects in an encrypted bucket come back with SSE response headers even when uploaded without them.
weed/s3api/s3_bucket_encryption.go.what: Parses and serves the ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration XML (only the first Rule is used: SSEAlgorithm AES256 or aws:kms, optional KMSMasterKeyID, BucketKeyEnabled), validates it, and stores it as the Encryption field of the bucket's protobuf metadata (Entry.Content) through UpdateBucketEncryption / ClearBucketEncryption in s3api_bucket_config.go. GetBucketEncryptionConfig is what putToFiler's applyBucketDefaultEncryption calls: an explicit bucket config wins; otherwise a table bucket's declared encryption (from its s3tables record) is reported; absence maps to ErrNoEncryptionConfig.
weed/s3api/s3_bucket_encryption.go.when: PUT/GET/DELETE /bucket?encryption (routed with ACTION_ADMIN); GetBucketEncryptionConfig on every PutObject/CopyObject that carries no explicit SSE headers (not on multipart parts).
weed/s3api/s3_bucket_encryption.go.why: Consequence: when this answers wrongly, objects written without SSE headers are stored in plaintext in a bucket the operator required to be encrypted, or writes fail. Design: GetBucketEncryptionConfig distinguishes 'no configuration' (write proceeds unencrypted) from a lookup error, which the write path turns into a failed PUT, so a transient filer error can never silently bypass default encryption. A table bucket's declared encryption cannot be deleted through this API (MethodNotAllowed), because it comes from the table bucket record. AWS compatibility: only one rule is honored, as in AWS; a missing configuration answers ServerSideEncryptionConfigurationNotFoundError.

weed/s3api/s3_constants/.character: Leaf package of constants and stateless helpers (no S3ApiServer dependency); imported by nearly every file in s3api and by other SeaweedFS packages; one process-wide atomic mode flag (backslash-in-key)
gotchas: NormalizeObjectKey turns '\' into '/' by default, unlike AWS, where they are distinct keys; the mode is process-wide and set once at startup.
ExtChecksum* keys deliberately use the x-seaweedfs- prefix so the generic metadata-to-header loop does not leak them to clients.
SeaweedFSPrincipalHeader and SeaweedFSSessionTokenHeader are trusted internal headers: every auth entry point must scrub client-supplied values (auth_credentials.go scrubInternalHeaders).
S3TABLES_ACTION_* must stay in sync with the dispatch switch in s3tables/handler.go (comment says it is the source of truth).
weed/s3api/s3_constants/.if_broken: Data written under old keys becomes unreadable as S3 state, internal headers could leak to clients or be accepted from them, and path traversal across buckets becomes possible.
weed/s3api/s3_constants/.ux: Invisible directly; it fixes key normalization (duplicate slashes collapsed, a leading slash dropped, '\' turned into '/' unless -s3.allowBackslashInKey) and which response headers clients see.
weed/s3api/s3_constants/.what: The shared vocabulary of the gateway: AWS header names (x-amz-*, SSE, checksum, object lock, conditional, copy-source, rename), the filer Extended-attribute keys SeaweedFS stores S3 state under (Seaweed-X-Amz-Versioning, -Version-Id, -Latest-Version-*, object-lock keys, x-seaweedfs-* internal keys), legacy action names (Read/Write/List/Admin/…) and s3:/s3tables: policy action strings, canned ACL grants, grantee groups, ownership modes, crypto sizes and SSE identifiers, folder names (.uploads, .versions, .system), DefaultBucketsPath and ObjectWriteRouteKeyPrefix. Helpers: GetBucketAndObject (mux vars + NormalizeObjectKey), IsValidObjectKey/IsValidBucketName/IsValidPathSegment (path-traversal guards), GetPrefix, EffectiveOwnership, and the request-context identity API (identity name, principal ARN, OIDC claim, access key id, stored credential, ignored session token) backed by a mutable identityHolder shared across request copies.
weed/s3api/s3_constants/.when: Read on every request (GetBucketAndObject from routing and auth; context helpers from auth, handlers and the audit log). SetAllowBackslashInObjectKey runs once at the end of server construction.
weed/s3api/s3_constants/.why: Consequence: these strings are an on-disk format. Changing an Ext* key orphans every bucket and object already written (versioning, lock and SSE state become invisible); changing a header name breaks client compatibility. Design: identity travels in context values, never headers, because headers can be spoofed; the identityHolder pointer exists because auth runs as an inner handler whose r.WithContext copy is invisible to outer middleware such as the audit logger. StoredCredentialFingerprint is an HMAC with a server key, because an unkeyed hash of the secret inside a vended token would give the token holder an offline guessing oracle. IsValidObjectKey rejects '.'/'..' segments and NUL after mux URL-decoding, because filepath.Join in the filer would otherwise collapse them and escape the bucket directory. AWS compatibility: PartOffsetMultiplier = 8 GiB per part (larger than the 5 GiB max part) keeps SSE CTR IVs from colliding across parts; absent or invalid ownership behaves as BucketOwnerEnforced.

weed/s3api/s3_error_utils.go.character: Two small error helpers: a not-found classifier for filer errors and the log-and-return pair used by the multipart engine
gotchas: On an error that is not a gRPC status at all, the function falls back to matching the sentinel's text anywhere in err.Error(), including client-chosen path text a caller wrapped in.
weed/s3api/s3_error_utils.go.if_broken: Transient filer failures surface as 404s, or real misses as 500s.
weed/s3api/s3_error_utils.go.ux: Correct NoSuchKey / NoSuchBucket versus InternalError answers.
weed/s3api/s3_error_utils.go.what: isFilerNotFound reports whether a filer error means 'not found': the filer_pb.ErrNotFound sentinel, a gRPC NotFound status, or an Unknown status whose message contains the sentinel's text (as list and cache errors arrive raw over gRPC). handleMultipartError logs and returns (nil, code); handleMultipartInternalError is the ErrInternalError shorthand.
weed/s3api/s3_error_utils.go.when: isFilerNotFound in filer_util, bucket and object handlers and retention; the multipart helpers throughout filer_multipart.go.
weed/s3api/s3_error_utils.go.why: Consequence: treating a failed read as 'absent' makes the gateway act on missing data (create over existing objects, answer NoSuchKey on a transient error), while the opposite turns every miss into a 500. Design: lookups are already normalized by filer_pb.LookupEntry, but list and cache errors are not, so the text is matched only on miss-shaped statuses and only on what the filer itself said, because callers wrap errors with client-chosen paths.

weed/s3api/s3_iam_middleware.go.character: S3IAMIntegration: the adapter between the S3 gateway and the advanced IAM manager (weed/iam/integration), implementing the IAMIntegration interface; one instance per server when -s3.iam.config / EnableIam is set
gotchas: AuthorizeAction returns ErrNone (allow) when the integration has no IAM manager (enabled=false).
Only the FIRST role in the token's 'roles' claim is used (selectPrimaryRole).
A literal token 'invalid-token' or any token shorter than 10 chars is rejected up front (test-shaped guard).

Unused leftovers: MockSessionInfo / MockAssumedRoleUser types, IAMIdentity.IsAdmin (always false), S3ApiServer.SetIAMIntegration (hard-codes 'localhost:8888', no non-test callers), and the 'requestTime' context value, which nothing sets.
External OIDC validation has a 15s timeout per request.
weed/s3api/s3_iam_middleware.go.if_broken: Federated access fails, or tokens are accepted for roles their trust policy does not allow.
weed/s3api/s3_iam_middleware.go.ux: Federated (OIDC) users can call S3 directly with their ID token, and role / attached-policy permissions apply like AWS IAM.
weed/s3api/s3_iam_middleware.go.what: AuthenticateJWT accepts 'Authorization: Bearer <OIDC token>' from an EXTERNAL issuer: it reads the issuer without verifying, validates the token through the STS service's web-identity providers, requires a user id and a role (first entry of the 'roles' claim), checks the role's trust policy for that web identity, and returns an IAMIdentity whose claims (email, name, groups, sub, role, iss, aws:userid, the trusted OIDC issuer list) feed policy variables. AuthorizeAction builds the request context (aws:SourceIp through trusted proxies, user agent, referer, s3:prefix for listings, claims also as jwt:<claim>), resolves the fine-grained action and resource ARN, and asks IAMManager.IsActionAllowed with the principal, session token and attached policy names. Also ValidateSessionToken (STS session tokens on SigV4 requests), ValidateTrustPolicyForPrincipal, DefaultAllow, buildS3ResourceArn and ParseUnverifiedJWTToken.
weed/s3api/s3_iam_middleware.go.when: authenticateRequestInternal for JWT bearer requests, authorizeWithIAM (auth_credentials.go) for identities routed to the IAM integration, verifyV4Signature for STS session tokens, and the explicit-deny checks.
weed/s3api/s3_iam_middleware.go.why: Consequence: OIDC/STS users, roles and attached IAM policies are authorized only through here; a mistake grants roles to the wrong users or denies every federated request. Design: the token's issuer is read unverified only to route it; real verification happens in the STS provider before anything is trusted. STS-issued tokens are rejected as Bearer tokens, so they must arrive as SigV4 + X-Amz-Security-Token, where the request signature binds them. Claims are exposed both bare and as jwt:<name> so AWS-style ${aws:...} and JWT-claim policy variables both resolve. AWS compatibility: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity semantics (trust policy check against the web identity) and s3:prefix conditions on ListBucket.

weed/s3api/s3_sse_c.go.character: Stateless SSE-C helpers (customer-provided AES-256 key) plus the shared decryptReaderCloser wrapper type
gotchas: SSE-C has no key commitment (the server never holds the key); integrity of the key choice rests on the stored KeyMD5.
An MD5 mismatch logs both the provided and expected MD5 values at error level.
decryptReaderCloser defined here is shared by the SSE-KMS and SSE-S3 decrypt paths to close the underlying HTTP body.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_c.go.if_broken: SSE-C objects become unreadable, or a wrong key is accepted and garbage is returned.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_c.go.ux: Clients must send the same key on every read; mismatches answer AccessDenied (stored MD5 differs) or the specific SSE-C errors.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_c.go.what: Parses and validates the three SSE-C headers (algorithm must be AES256, key must base64-decode to 32 bytes, and its base64 MD5 must equal x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-key-MD5), for the target and for the copy source (x-amz-copy-source-server-side-encryption-customer-*). Encrypts with AES-256-CTR and a random IV per object or part; decrypts with the stored IV, optionally advancing the counter to an offset inside the part (CreateSSECDecryptedReaderWithOffset). Decides copy strategy (Direct only when source, copy-source key and destination key all have the same MD5), and maps SSE-C errors to S3 codes.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_c.go.when: PUT/UploadPart/Copy with SSE-C headers, and every GET/HEAD of an SSE-C object (the key must be resent on each request).
weed/s3api/s3_sse_c.go.why: Consequence: the gateway never stores the customer key, only its MD5, so a wrong key must be detected through the MD5 comparison or the object would decrypt to garbage. Design: each part gets its own random IV (unlike SSE-KMS/S3's base IV + offset), and per-chunk metadata records the PartOffset within that part's stream. AWS compatibility: all three headers are required together; SSE-C and SSE-KMS headers are mutually exclusive (a KMS algorithm or key id makes IsSSECRequest false); copies of SSE-C objects need the copy-source key headers.

weed/s3api/s3_sse_kms.go.character: Stateless crypto helpers for SSE-KMS (AES-256-CTR with a KMS-wrapped per-object data key) plus metadata (de)serialization and copy-strategy decisions shared by all three SSE types
gotchas: Multipart SSE-KMS stores the BASE IV with ChunkOffset; CreateSSEKMSDecryptedReader applies the offset. Never pre-adjust the IV before calling it.
Objects written before key commitments shipped have none; whether they are accepted depends on RequireKeyCommitmentEnv (s3_validation_utils.go).
DeserializeSSEKMSMetadata defaults a missing algorithm to aws:kms but rejects any other algorithm.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_kms.go.if_broken: Encrypted objects cannot be read back, wrong-key reads succeed with garbage, or copies silently drop or double-apply encryption.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_kms.go.issue_note: The S3 Bucket Key optimization is not wired in: CreateSSEKMSEncryptedReaderWithBucketKey forces bucketKeyEnabled=false ('not fully implemented yet'), and the per-bucket data-key cache path (CreateSSEKMSEncryptedReaderForBucket → getBucketKMSCache → getBucketDataKey, plus CleanupBucketKMSCache / CleanupAllBucketKMSCaches and BucketKMSCache in s3api_bucket_config.go) has no non-test callers. It also carries a latent bug if revived: CreateSSEKMSEncryptedReaderForBucket defers kms.ClearSensitiveData(dataKeyResp.Plaintext) on a response that may come from the cache, zeroing the cached key for every later hit; and getBucketKMSCache assigns KMSKeyCache on the shared cached BucketConfig without a lock.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_kms.go.ux: SSE-KMS works with any configured KMS provider (aws, gcp, local, openbao); clients see x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms and the key id; KMS failures map to KMSKeyNotFound / KMSAccessDenied / KMSKeyDisabledException / InvalidCiphertext.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_kms.go.what: Encrypts with a fresh KMS data key and a random 16-byte IV (CreateSSEKMSEncryptedReaderWithBucketKey) or with a base IV advanced to a part offset for multipart (…WithBaseIVAndOffset); decrypts by asking the configured KMS provider to unwrap the data key, checking the returned KeyID and the HMAC key commitment, then applying ChunkOffset to the stored base IV (CreateSSEKMSDecryptedReader). Serializes SSEKMSKey to JSON metadata (algorithm, keyId, wrapped key, encryption context, IV, partOffset, keyCommitment) and also defines SSECMetadata (per-chunk SSE-C IV/keyMD5/partOffset). Response headers, request detection, KMS error→S3 error mapping, encryption-context parsing (base64 JSON, ≤256-char keys and values), and the copy strategy decisions (DetermineSSEKMSCopyStrategy, DetermineUnifiedCopyStrategy: Direct / Encrypt / Decrypt / Reencrypt / KeyRotation).
weed/s3api/s3_sse_kms.go.when: PUT/UploadPart/Copy with x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms or under a KMS bucket default; GET/HEAD/range reads of KMS objects (per-chunk metadata in s3api_object_handlers.go); copy paths choose a strategy here.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_kms.go.why: Consequence: every SSE-KMS object depends on this exact metadata format and IV scheme; a change makes existing objects undecryptable. Design: the key commitment binds the data key to the IV and algorithm, so a swapped wrapped key or IV is rejected instead of decrypting to garbage; the KeyID returned by KMS must match the stored one. Copies between objects under the same KMS key can reuse ciphertext (Direct) instead of decrypting and re-encrypting. AWS compatibility: SSE-KMS requests are recognized only when no SSE-C algorithm header is present (the two are mutually exclusive); the encryption context travels base64-encoded JSON like AWS's x-amz-server-side-encryption-context.

weed/s3api/s3_sse_s3.go.character: SSE-S3 crypto helpers plus SSES3KeyManager, a process-global singleton (globalSSES3KeyManager) that holds the cluster KEK ('super key') behind an RWMutex
gotchas: GetOrCreateKey ignores its keyID and always generates a new DEK; StoreKey is a no-op. Keys live only inside the per-object metadata.
loadFilerKEK retries the filer 10 times at 2s intervals (up to ~20s of startup delay) before failing.
GetSSES3IV falls back to the FIRST chunk's metadata IV when the object-level key has none.
Multipart SSE-S3 stores the already-ADJUSTED IV per chunk (CreateSSES3EncryptedReaderWithBaseIV returns the derived IV); decrypt uses it as-is, unlike SSE-KMS.
KeyID is 'sse-s3-key-<math/rand Int63>': an identifier, not a secret.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_s3.go.if_broken: All SSE-S3 objects become unreadable (wrong or missing KEK), or new objects get encrypted under a key that does not match the cluster's, so they are unreadable from other gateways.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_s3.go.ux: With no KEK configured, SSE-S3 requests fail with a clear 'set s3.sse.kek or s3.sse.key' error instead of silently storing plaintext; operators see migration warnings in logs.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_s3.go.what: Every SSE-S3 object gets a fresh random 256-bit data key (DEK) and AES-256-CTR stream (random IV, or base IV + offset for multipart parts). SerializeSSES3Metadata wraps the DEK with the KEK using AES-GCM and stores {algorithm, keyId, encryptedDEK, nonce, iv, keyCommitment} as JSON; DeserializeSSES3Metadata unwraps it. The KEK comes from exactly one source, resolved at startup in InitializeWithFiler: security.toml s3.sse.kek (hex, verified against any existing filer KEK), s3.sse.key (any string, HKDF-derived; refused while a filer KEK exists), or the legacy /etc/s3/sse_kek file on the filer, wrapped with an HKDF(passphrase)-derived AES-GCM key when s3.sse.kek.passphrase / WEED_S3_SSE_KEK_PASSPHRASE is set. Legacy plaintext and fixed-salt v1 wraps are migrated to the random-salt v2 format ('SWv2'). GetMasterKey derives an STS signing key from the KEK via HKDF.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_s3.go.when: InitializeGlobalSSES3KeyManager runs early in NewS3ApiServerWithStore (before IAM, because STS may fall back to the KEK). Encrypt and decrypt run on PUT/UploadPart/Copy with AES256 or under an AES256 bucket default, and on every read of SSE-S3 data.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_s3.go.why: Consequence: the KEK is the root of every SSE-S3 object; losing or changing it makes all of them undecryptable, so the resolver refuses configurations that would silently switch keys (configured KEK ≠ filer KEK, or a derived key while a filer KEK exists). Design: envelope encryption means each object has its own DEK and only the small wrapped DEK depends on the KEK; GCM authenticates the wrap; the key commitment rejects DEK/IV mismatches. A KEK stored in plaintext on the filer is readable by anyone with filer access, hence the passphrase wrap and the automatic migration with warnings. The STS fallback uses an HKDF derivation so the raw KEK is never used as a signing key. AWS compatibility: SSE-S3 is x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256 with server-managed keys, matching AWS semantics.

weed/s3api/s3_sse_utils.go.character: Single stateless function shared by SSE-KMS and SSE-S3: CTR counter arithmetic
gotchas: A base IV that is not 16 bytes is returned unchanged with skip 0 (logged), not rejected.
The carry propagates only through the low 8 bytes, while Go's CTR increments all 16; the two diverge only if the low 64 bits of the IV overflow within one object (negligible for random IVs).
weed/s3api/s3_sse_utils.go.if_broken: Encrypted multipart objects and range reads return corrupted plaintext, or counters are reused across parts.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_utils.go.ux: Invisible; correct ranged and multipart reads of encrypted objects.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_utils.go.what: calculateIVWithOffset(baseIV, offset) returns the AES-CTR IV for the 16-byte block containing `offset` (adding offset/16 to the low 64 bits of the IV, big-endian, with carry) and the intra-block skip offset%16.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_utils.go.when: SSE-KMS decrypt when ChunkOffset > 0, SSE-S3 per-chunk IV derivation at write time, multipart part encryption with a base IV, and range reads.
weed/s3api/s3_sse_utils.go.why: Consequence: multipart and per-chunk SSE depend on deriving, for any byte offset, the same counter the encrypting stream had there; a mismatch decrypts to garbage. Design: deriving IVs from one base IV plus an offset avoids storing an IV per byte range and, combined with the 8 GiB PartOffsetMultiplier per part (larger than the 5 GiB max part), guarantees parts never reuse a counter, which in CTR mode would leak plaintext XORs.

weed/s3api/s3_validation_utils.go.character: Stateless SSE validation helpers plus one process-wide atomic flag (requireKeyCommitment) initialized from the environment
gotchas: The strict flag is read from the environment once in init(); changing it later needs SetRequireKeyCommitment.
weed/s3api/s3_validation_utils.go.if_broken: Tampered encryption metadata goes undetected, or every legacy encrypted object becomes unreadable.
weed/s3api/s3_validation_utils.go.ux: Invisible unless the strict flag is on and a legacy object is read (it then fails with a clear error).
weed/s3api/s3_validation_utils.go.what: ComputeKeyCommitment / VerifyKeyCommitment: HMAC-SHA256(key, IV||algorithm) stored next to the IV and checked in constant time on decrypt. A missing commitment is accepted (legacy objects) unless WEED_S3_REQUIRE_KEY_COMMITMENT=true or SetRequireKeyCommitment(true). Also isValidKMSKeyID (non-empty, no spaces or control characters, ≤500 chars), ValidateIV (exactly 16 bytes), ValidateSSEKMSKey (non-nil), ValidateSSES3Key (32-byte key, AES256, key id set, optional 16-byte IV).
weed/s3api/s3_validation_utils.go.when: Every SSE-KMS / SSE-S3 decrypt (VerifyKeyCommitment), every encrypt (ComputeKeyCommitment), and KMS key id parsing from requests and bucket encryption configs.
weed/s3api/s3_validation_utils.go.why: Consequence: AES-CTR is unauthenticated; without a commitment, someone with write access to object metadata could swap the key reference or IV and make the gateway decrypt to attacker-chosen garbage without any error. Design: the commitment binds ciphertext parameters to the exact key; the strict flag lets operators close the downgrade path of stripping the commitment once legacy objects are re-encrypted. AWS compatibility: the permissive default keeps objects written before commitments readable; KMS key ids are validated loosely (MinIO-style) so any provider's id format works.

weed/s3api/s3api_acl_helper.go.character: Stateless S3 ACL library (parse, validate, store, render) plus the AccountManager interface it resolves grantees through (implemented by IdentityAccessManagement)
gotchas: Canned ACLs append the package-level grant pointers from s3_constants (PublicRead etc.); mutating a returned grant would mutate the shared defaults.
aclOwnerAccountManager lets the request's own owner id resolve as a valid grantee even if the identity store has no display name for it.
When putAcl is true (PutBucketAcl / PutObjectAcl header form) custom x-amz-grant-* headers are ignored by ParseAclHeaders; only the canned ACL is parsed.
weed/s3api/s3api_acl_helper.go.if_broken: Objects or buckets become public unintentionally, legitimate grants are rejected, or GetAcl output breaks SDK parsing.
weed/s3api/s3api_acl_helper.go.ux: x-amz-acl, x-amz-grant-* and ACL XML bodies behave as on AWS; Get*Acl shows display names resolved from the identity store.
weed/s3api/s3api_acl_helper.go.what: Parses ACLs from an AccessControlPolicy XML body (owner must match) or from headers: x-amz-grant-* lists of id="…" / emailAddress="…" / uri="…" pairs (strict JSON-quoted values) or one canned ACL (private, public-read, public-read-write, authenticated-read, log-delivery-write, bucket-owner-read, bucket-owner-full-control; aws-exec-read → NotImplemented), applying ownership rules (bucket-owner-full-control under BucketOwnerPreferred hands ownership to the bucket owner). ValidateAndTransferGrants checks every grantee exists (canonical id known, group URI one of AllUsers/AuthenticatedUsers/LogDelivery, email resolvable) and converts email grantees to canonical ids. AssembleEntryWithAcp / GetAcpGrants store and read grants as JSON in Seaweed-X-Amz-Acl (owner in Seaweed-X-Amz-Owner); buildAccessControlList renders the AWS XML.
weed/s3api/s3api_acl_helper.go.when: PutBucket / PutBucketAcl / PutObjectAcl, upload ACL preparation (s3api_object_upload_acl.go), Get*Acl rendering, and the anonymous-read path (public grant detection).
weed/s3api/s3api_acl_helper.go.why: Consequence: ACLs decide public visibility (AllUsers READ makes objects readable anonymously); a parsing bug can make private data public or lock out the owner. Design: grantees are validated against known accounts so a typo cannot create a grant to a non-existent principal; emails are normalized to ids at write time so later account email changes do not alter grants. AWS compatibility: the canned ACL semantics and grant-header syntax follow the S3 spec.
